articles.description: If robots.txt returns a 503 error, restore delivery of the intended crawl rules before rewriting your...
articles.body_html:
If robots.txt returns a 503 error, restore delivery of the intended crawl rules before rewriting your product pages. A working homepage does not show that Google can retrieve the rules for that host. Treat the rules endpoint and the content endpoints as separate checks, then verify crawl activity after the delivery problem is fixed.

This is a specific technical discovery problem. It can interrupt the route to Google Search even when the page itself looks healthy. It does not prove why a brand is missing from ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini, and the behavior described here should not be applied to every crawler.

The incident below is hypothetical. It shows how to organize an investigation without claiming that a real site was tested or that repairing one response guarantees indexing, rankings or AI citations.

Distinguish an unavailable rule file from a blocking rule

A 503 response and an intentional Disallow directive describe different conditions. One says the server could not deliver a resource. The other is a rule inside a delivered file. Editing the text of a file is unlikely to solve a request that never reaches that file.

Google's robots.txt specification describes an initial 12-hour crawl pause after server errors, with continued attempts to fetch the file. Later behavior depends on cached rules, elapsed time and site availability. Read the documented sequence rather than treating a 503 as an immediate permanent removal.

Start the incident record with the observed response, not an assumed policy. Write “the rules request returned 503 at this time” instead of “Google is blocked.” The narrower statement gives engineering a condition it can reproduce and avoids confusing delivery failure with an editorial or indexing decision.

Check the exact public host and request

Record the complete robots.txt URL, including protocol and hostname. The rules for the marketing host and the documentation host may be separate. A successful check on one is not a substitute for checking the other. Include any port that is part of the public address.

Use a normal GET request to inspect the status and returned content. Record redirects, response headers, the final URL and a short description of the body. A status-only probe can miss an application error page that was returned with an apparently successful status.

Keep the record small enough to compare across checks. Useful fields include time, host, request method, observed status, response type, relevant cache information and the intended rules version. Do not put credentials, private cookies or unrelated request data into a public incident write-up.

Trace the layer that produced the response

Compare the response at the public edge with what the origin would return through your approved diagnostic process. The edge is the layer users and crawlers normally reach first, such as a content delivery network or gateway. The origin is the service behind it.

If the origin serves the intended file while the public endpoint returns an error, inspect the route between them. Look for a failed deployment, a route accidentally handled by the application, an unavailable dependency or a cached error. These are investigation candidates, not a diagnosis established by the mismatch alone.

If both layers fail, follow the request through the service that owns the resource. Assign the endpoint an owner. A small text file can become an unowned dependency when marketing assumes infrastructure serves it and infrastructure assumes the web application does.

Work through a bounded incident example

Imagine a fictional SaaS site with a marketing homepage and public documentation on the same host. After a release, the homepage returns its normal content, but the robots.txt request returns a 503 page generated by a gateway. The team first notices fewer crawler requests in its logs.

The tempting response is to change the documentation headings or remove restrictions from the file. Neither follows from the evidence yet. The initial question is whether the deployed route can deliver the approved rules. The team compares the current route configuration with the last working deployment and checks whether the file depends on the failing application service.

Suppose, within this example, the route was unintentionally changed to forward the request through that service. Restoring the intended delivery path addresses the observed failure. It does not establish that every later traffic change came from this incident. The example ends with a verifiable request result, not an invented ranking recovery.

Preserve the policy while restoring delivery

Use the approved file as the reference for the repair. Check the expected groups, paths and sitemap entries against the intended version. Avoid replacing the file with an empty response simply because that removes the immediate server error. Availability and policy correctness are separate requirements.

Review the change with whoever owns crawler policy. A technical incident should not quietly expand what can be crawled. Equally, a broad temporary restriction should not become permanent because nobody schedules its review. Record both the operational repair and any deliberate policy change as distinct decisions.

Google's documentation also distinguishes most 4xx responses from server errors. Do not manufacture a 404 or 403 as a shortcut around a broken delivery path. Choose the response that accurately represents the intended resource and verify the relevant provider's interpretation before changing its status behavior.

Use two recovery gates

The first gate is delivery recovery. Repeated checks should reach the correct endpoint and receive the intended rules, without the earlier error or an unexpected application page. Check the affected public host and relevant edge locations available through your normal monitoring. Save enough evidence to identify the deployed version.

The second gate is observed crawler recovery. Check fresh request logs and Google's Crawl Stats report for the affected property. That report includes host availability information and crawl responses. Its reporting window is different from a direct request made now, so compare timestamps before describing a mismatch as a new failure.

Passing the first gate does not automatically pass the second. Nor does resumed crawling prove indexing or a ranking improvement. Keep the incident's completion criteria separate from the longer search-performance review. Otherwise a team may reopen a fixed delivery incident because an unrelated commercial metric has not moved.

Compare the evidence before and after the repair

Keep a short before-and-after record for the endpoint, the rules content and the crawler observations. State which observations were available and which were not. If logs are missing for part of the incident, leave that period unknown rather than reconstructing a precise outage from memory.

Check a representative content URL as well. The rules can recover while the page still has its own delivery or indexing problem. Conversely, the page may have stayed available throughout. Reporting those separately makes the scope of the incident clear to content and marketing teams.

If another AI or search crawler appears relevant to the business question, investigate it as a separate provider-specific task. Do not infer its caching or error handling from Googlebot's documented sequence. A shared file format does not establish identical operational behavior across products.

Make the rules endpoint part of release verification

Add the public robots.txt endpoint to the checks you already perform after routing, hosting or gateway changes. Verify its content as well as its status. The useful assertion is that the approved rules remain available at the intended address after a real deployment.

Keep monitoring proportionate to the site. A small business does not need a sprawling crawler dashboard to notice that one important endpoint has stopped working. It needs a clear owner, a repeatable check and an alert that reaches someone able to repair the route.

For the next investigation, start with one question: did the crawler receive the rules you intended to serve? Once that answer is supported, decide whether the remaining problem concerns access, page delivery, indexing or content. That order keeps a small infrastructure failure from turning into a week of unsupported copy changes.

articles.title: I Built the Study Buddy I Wish I Had the Night Before Exams- Meet Study Sloth: An AI Study Buddy That Takes Care of the Busywork 🦥📚
articles.description: This is my submission for Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady. PRESENTING...
articles.body_html:
This is my submission for Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady.
PRESENTING ~~ [www.studysloth.tech]

Study Sloth: for the student with 8 units, 4 lab records and 1 night left

It's 11:47 PM. Your exam is at 9 AM.
You have a 90-minute lecture recording you never rewatched, a PDF called unit3_FINAL_final2.pdf, a lab record due in the morning, and a group chat full of people asking "does anyone have notes?"

If that made your stomach drop a little, this post is for you. I built Study Sloth because I've been that student.

Sound familiar?

1. The 90-minute recording you will never rewatch.
You were in the lecture. You still don't know what was taught. The recording sits in a folder, quietly judging you.

2. Your material lives in six places.
Board photos in the gallery, PDFs named unit3_FINAL_final2.pdf, half-written notes in a chat with yourself. And at 1 AM, 40 people ask the group: "does anyone have the Unit 3 notes?"

3. The notes that cost me marks.
I once leaned on last-minute AI notes. They were correct, but they weren't what my teacher had taught, so I lost marks for things that weren't wrong, just never taught. (I was too smart to pay attention in class. Lesson learned, painfully.)

4. Flashcards that take longer to make than to study.
You spend the whole evening formatting cards, then have no time left to learn a single one.

5. The lab record. Again. And then the viva.
The same template every time: rewrite the aim, theory, procedure and conclusion, paste the code and output, fight the formatting. Then the examiner asks, "Why did you use a LEFT JOIN here?" About your own code. "Because it worked" is not an answer.

Five problems. One night. Zero chill.

So I built the buddy I wanted

I went looking for a tool that did all this. Umm, I couldn't find one. So, as the wise developers once said:

BUILD IT.

...and that's exactly what I did.

Study Sloth is a study workspace that does the setup work, so you can get to the learning sooner. It doesn't learn for you. It turns what you already have into what you need.

Here's how it answers each of those:

The pain What Study Sloth does
The recording you won't rewatch Turns it into a timestamped transcript and notes by unit
Material in six places One subject folder per course: syllabus, lectures, PDFs, labs and cards, with PDFs turned into notes with page references
Notes that weren't what was taught Works from your lectures and your PDFs, and every point carries a timestamp or page number so you can check it
Flashcard-making Generates flashcards, quizzes and likely viva questions in the same step
The lab record and the viva Builds a lab manual from your experiment titles, using your real outputs when you have them. Its questions flow into the Study Deck, so you can practise "why did I do this?"

It's also the one-night-before-exams buddy for people who work best under pressure (hi, it's me). Just don't make it your only plan.

What I Built

  • Organise a course: turn a syllabus into units and topics.
  • Study from PDFs: upload a text-based PDF and get structured notes with page references.
  • Review lectures: turn audio or video into a timestamped transcript, then notes by unit.
  • Practise actively: flashcards, quizzes, and likely viva questions.
  • Prepare lab records: build a manual from your experiment titles. Use your real outputs when you have them. When you don't, the manual can include generated expected outputs, labelled as expected, not yours.
  • Keep revision connected: lab-manual flashcards and quizzes appear in the same Study Deck.

There are three ways to use it, and they handle your data differently:

Version What it does Where your data goes
Local app Everything: lectures, PDFs, labs, study deck Stays on your computer (local Ollama and Whisper)
Hosted workspace (Render) The full interface in a browser Text goes to [model provider]; recordings go to Groq for transcription; data is temporary
Lightweight notes page PDF or pasted text in, study set out Text goes to [model provider]; nothing is stored

Demo

  • Live: - [studysloth.tech]/[www.studysloth.tech]
  • Code: The source is available here:

AaliyaKhan25 / Study-Sloth

Hacktober Fest 2k26

Study Sloth

Turn study material into a study plan you can actually use.

Study Sloth is an AI-assisted study workspace that transforms notes, syllabi, lectures, and lab work into organized learning materials—so students can spend less time formatting and more time understanding.

Features · Get started · AI models · Deployment · Contributing


Why Study Sloth?

Studying often means jumping between lecture files, notes, flashcards, quizzes, code, and lab-record templates. Study Sloth brings those tasks together in one calm, student-focused interface. Add your material and build a useful next step from it: clearer notes, revision questions, or a structured lab record.

The project has three ways to use it:


























Experience Best for Entry point
Local Study Sloth A personal workspace, including video/audio lecture transcription and lab tools app.main:app
Hosted Study Sloth A browser-based workspace hosted on Render web:app
Study Sloth Online A lightweight notes-and-PDF study-material generator online:app

The hosted and…


View on GitHub


Also, do check out my GitHub Profile: [https://github.com/AaliyaKhan25]

A note on the live version: on Render's free tier, the filesystem is temporary, so workspaces and uploads can disappear after a restart. It's a demo, not a vault.

How I Built It

Python, FastAPI, SQLite, and plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Slow work (transcription, long PDFs) runs as background jobs, so the browser shows progress instead of waiting on one long request.

  • Study material: Gemma 4:cloud and Gemma3:4b , through an Ollama-compatible API. The text model and the vision model are separate settings, so either can be swapped by changing one value.
  • Transcription: locally, faster-whisper on the GPU. Hosted, Groq's whisper-large-v3-turbo, because running Whisper on a small Render plan wasn't practical. The trade-off: recordings are sent to Groq, uploads are limited to 25 MB, and quotas may apply.
  • Checkable notes: every point keeps its timestamp or page number.
  • Lab records: you can enter your own outputs, and you confirm and review the record before printing.

What Went Wrong (and What I Learned)

1. "New" doesn't mean "compatible." Video uploads failed with TypeError: open() got an unexpected keyword argument 'metadata_errors', even though PyAV was already very recent. Reproducing the exact call showed the installed PyAV rejected the keyword; faster-whisper passed. I pinned a compatible range, added a regression test, and added a CPU fallback for when CUDA is detected, but its libraries are missing. "Upgrade everything" wasn't the fix.

2. The cloud changes what "local" means. Once the app was hosted, labels like "stays on this computer" became untrue, and file paths broke. One Render deploy built fine and then crashed at startup because /var/data wasn't a mounted disk. The app now falls back to temporary storage with a warning, and the hosted page rewrites its labels to say what really happens to your data.

3. Keep visitors' workspaces apart. Hosted visitors get a cookie-based workspace. Python's contextvars don't follow work into worker threads, so I copy the request context into each job. This isn't an account system: there's no sign-in, so treat a workspace as private-ish, not a secure vault.

4. Failures should be loud. An early version swallowed model errors, so a broken job looked like an empty result. Now a failed job shows its real error in the app. The tests cover the awkward paths too: transcription fallback, Groq response handling, a missing disk path, and manually linked cards. All 9 pass locally, which proves those code paths, not that the public deployment is live.

How I Used GitHub Copilot

I used GitHub Copilot in VS Code while building and debugging, for example, on the PyAV problem, the hosted-service behaviour, tests, and docs. GitHub Actions also ran the tests on every push. Copilot helped build the app; Gemma is the model inside it. They do different jobs.

Why Open Innovation Matters

Studying shouldn't depend on one closed assistant that you can't inspect, can't run offline, and can't afford when the free plan runs out. Open models let me choose the tool for the job and the hardware. Because the model is just a setting, I could run Gemma locally for privacy and still point the hosted version at a different provider.

That also means "open" doesn't mean "everything on one server". Gemma writes the study material and Groq handles hosted transcription, so users should know which service sees what. Being honest about that trade-off is part of building with open tools.

The Lazy Payoff

I won't invent a "minutes saved" number. [Time one real lecture or PDF and add it: "A 10-minute lecture became unit-wise notes, 8 flashcards and 5 quiz questions in X minutes."]. The aim is fewer blank-page moments: source material in, a first draft of notes and practice out.

If you try it, tell me which pain point it fixed for you, and which one it still doesn't.

Prize Categories

  • Best Use of Gemma: Gemma 3 4B is the default model for study material.
  • Best Use of a .tech Domain: [www.studysloth.tech]. It's my first domain, and a .tech one. Thank you, Hacktoberfest and MLH!
  • Best Use of GitHub Copilot: - Lifesaver for me; helped me resolve a hell lot of bugs. TYSM GitHub Copilot
  • Best Use of Render: - My deployment buddy for life , not just Hacktober; Render has always been there

Study smarter. Stay curious. Let the Sloth handle the busywork.

articles.title: Product Demo Captions: Review the Words and the Interface Together
articles.description: Review product demo captions against both the final audio and the interface before sharing the clip...
articles.body_html:
Review product demo captions against both the final audio and the interface before sharing the clip in public. Check names, negation, timing and the controls hidden by the text. Then watch the actual uploaded version, with captions enabled, and verify that a viewer can understand the task you are asking them to review.

A founder's demo is an invitation to examine work. If the caption changes “do not send” to “send,” or covers the result being discussed, the feedback may concern a different task from the one you intended. Caption review belongs beside the product walkthrough, rather than being treated as a final decorative layer.

Start with a task and a truthful ending

Imagine a fictional project tool that saves a request as a draft before someone sends it to a colleague. The public clip demonstrates creating the draft and reviewing its status. It does not demonstrate a successful delivery. All interface examples here are invented for that walkthrough; no video or accessibility audit was performed for this article.

Write down the ending before recording: the request exists as a saved draft and has not been sent. That gives the narration and caption review a concrete reference. A vague objective such as “show the new request flow” leaves room for an attractive edit to imply a later result.

Use sample content suited to public display. Keep the same sample throughout the clip so a viewer can follow the transition. If the request name changes halfway through, a caption correction will not explain whether the recording shows one journey or two different attempts.

Understand what the captions need to carry

W3C WAI's caption guidance describes captions as synchronized text for speech and the non-speech audio needed to understand the content. It distinguishes captions viewers can turn on and off from open captions that remain visible. It also explains that automatic output needs its accuracy confirmed.

Apply those principles to the actual recording. Review the final soundtrack, including any meaningful audio cue, rather than assuming the original script still matches after editing. A draft transcript can help with preparation, but the released clip is the reference you need to check.

Captions and visual explanation solve different gaps. If the recording silently changes a request from unsaved to saved, accurate speech captions alone may not communicate that change. Make the narration describe the important result, and consider the other accessibility needs of the complete media. This workflow is a focused review, not a claim of conformance.

Check the words that can reverse the action

In the fictional demo, the narrator says, “Save this as a draft. Do not send it yet.” A missing “not” reverses the instruction. Review that sentence against the audio and the visible state, rather than judging whether the caption merely looks grammatical.

Also check product terms and button names. If the actual control says “Save draft,” a caption reading “safe draft” can make the instruction harder to follow. Preserve the wording that helps a viewer connect the spoken explanation to the interface. Do not silently replace a term with a familiar one if the product uses something else.

Keep a short correction note with the affected moment, the incorrect text and the checked replacement. This gives a teammate something specific to verify. It also helps when a later edit reuses part of the clip and accidentally restores an earlier automatic transcript.

Match timing to the visible sequence

Watch the caption appear and disappear while following the task. A correct sentence displayed after the interface has moved on can describe the wrong control. A sentence that vanishes before it can be read may leave the viewer guessing about a consequential step.

For the fictional request, keep the explanation of the unsent state near the visible saved-draft result. If the edit jumps straight from clicking the save control to a different screen, restore enough context to make the result understandable. A caption should not be used to claim a state the footage never shows.

Check transitions after every cut that affects the audio or task order. Moving a pause can change the relationship between a sentence and a screen. Review the clip at its normal playback speed before using slower inspection to locate a specific defect. The intended viewer should not need an editing timeline to follow the explanation.

Leave the controls and result readable

Caption text shares space with small interface labels. Inspect whether it covers the control being named, the selected option or the final status. A caption placed over “Draft saved” removes the very evidence the walkthrough is meant to show.

In the fictional layout, reserve room for readable text without hiding the request card. If the player or publishing format changes the available space, adjust the recording composition or supported caption placement. Do not assume that a comfortable editing preview predicts the uploaded display.

Check the viewing conditions you expect people to use. A wide desktop recording may become difficult to read in a narrow feed. Record that limitation in the post if it remains relevant, and provide an appropriate route to a fuller explanation. Making text larger cannot recover an important control that has been cropped out entirely.

Review the uploaded clip as a separate artifact

After upload, enable the caption track in the actual player and watch the complete task. Confirm that the corrected version is the one available there. If the platform offers generated captions as well as an uploaded track, check which one is being displayed instead of assuming your file became the default.

Verify the first screen, the action and the ending together. In the fictional demo, the result should still be a draft, with no suggestion that the request reached another person. Check that the surrounding post describes the same boundary.

Keep a record of the uploaded version and the checks performed. A local export can be correct while a different file or older track is published. Reopen the public or saved preview through the normal site controls. An upload-complete message establishes that a transfer finished; it does not establish that the caption text and product claim agree.

Ask founder peers for a focused review

I build Buildside. Its public description includes founders sharing work and finding concrete help. A task-specific demo gives a peer something more useful to inspect than a request for general praise.

Ask the reviewer to describe the ending they understood and identify any moment when the text hid or contradicted the action. Let them report an uncertainty without explaining it away. If they think the fictional request was sent, inspect the footage, narration and surrounding post together.

A peer noticing a caption defect is a useful observation about this clip. It does not establish that all intended users understand the product or that the product itself is accessible. Keep media review, task usability and a wider accessibility evaluation as distinct pieces of work with their own evidence.

Keep the text aligned when the product changes

If a control is renamed or the flow changes, review the clip before continuing to distribute it as current guidance. Decide whether it needs a new recording, a dated explanation or removal from an active help path. Correct captions cannot make outdated footage describe today's interface.

When you publish a replacement, keep the correction specific. State which task or screen changed rather than suggesting the whole previous explanation was unusable. Update the entry points you control so a new reader can find the version that matches the current product.

Before sharing the next public demo, watch the uploaded task once with captions enabled and once while concentrating on the spoken explanation. Check that both accounts agree with the visible result. That gives other founders a clearer artifact to question and a more reliable starting point for feedback.

articles.title: Empty State Design: Show the Blank Screen When You Build in Public
articles.description: When you share a product demo while building in public, show the empty screen as well as the...
articles.body_html:
When you share a product demo while building in public, show the empty screen as well as the populated one. Explain why it is empty and give the viewer a relevant next action. First use and a search with no matching results can look similar while requiring different help, so review them as separate states.

A polished demo full of prepared records answers one question: what does the product look like once useful content is present? A new user may arrive before that point. A founder peer can give more focused feedback when the public walkthrough includes the conditions behind the blank screen and the task that should follow it.

Start with two blank screens that mean different things

Consider a fictional request tracker for small agencies. A newly created workspace contains no client requests. Later, a workspace with existing requests can also show an empty list when the user filters for a category that has no matches. Both views have zero visible rows, but the underlying situations are different.

In the first case, the user needs a route to creating or importing the first request. In the second, the user needs to understand the active filter and how to change it. Sending both people through the same welcome tour would ignore the task they are actually trying to complete.

Vercel's Geist empty-state guidance distinguishes first-use blank slates from no-results, cleared, permission and failed-load states. Use that distinction to plan what you will show publicly. The example here is an editorial walkthrough plan, not a claim that this fictional tracker has been implemented or tested.

Name the state before choosing the message

For each empty view, write a short explanation of the condition that produces it. In the fictional tracker, the first condition is an authorized user opening a new workspace with no requests created. The second is an authorized user applying a filter to a workspace that already contains other requests.

Keep permission and loading failures out of those labels. A request that failed to load does not establish that no records exist. A person without access should not be told to create the first item if the records are present but unavailable to them. Those states need their own accurate explanations.

This note can stay simple. Record the starting data, the relevant role, the action that produced the screen and the expected next step. You are making the public example understandable, not publishing internal identifiers or a complete account configuration.

Write the first-use state around the first useful action

A vague fictional message would say “Nothing here yet” above a button labelled Continue. A viewer cannot tell what belongs on the screen or what the button will do. An attractive illustration does not resolve that missing task information.

A more specific version is “No client requests yet,” followed by a sentence explaining that this list will hold incoming work. A primary action labelled “Create a request” names the next step. If importing existing requests is a supported alternative, explain that route without presenting several equally prominent choices.

Geist's guidance describes informational empty states as a place to explain a feature's usefulness and provide an action. Its component rules favor a clear primary action. Apply the principle to your actual workflow, then verify where the control leads. The wording alone does not prove that someone can complete the task.

Give a filtered-empty view a different route back

Now imagine the fictional workspace contains requests, but none match an active “Waiting for client” filter. Reusing “No client requests yet” would describe the workspace incorrectly. It could lead a user to create duplicate work because the screen hides the condition that removed the existing rows.

A suitable hypothetical message is “No requests match this filter,” with the active filter visible and an action to clear it. The user should be able to predict that clearing the filter will show the broader list, rather than adding a new item or resetting the whole workspace.

If the product supports several filters, check which ones remain active after a change. A public screenshot of one empty result may omit another constraint elsewhere in the interface. Include enough visible context for a peer to understand why the result is empty without sharing real client records.

Prepare a short walkthrough with a checkable ending

Use fictional records and a safe workspace you are authorized to show. Start the first-use walkthrough with the empty list, explain its condition, activate the named action and complete one sample request. Reopen the list so the viewer can see the resulting item in the place the message described.

For the filtered-empty walkthrough, begin with the same known set of sample requests. Apply the chosen filter, show the no-results message, clear the filter and confirm that the broader list returns. This sequence checks the specific promise made by the empty-state action.

Keep a note of what you actually observed. A recording can show that the demonstrated path worked under those conditions. It does not establish that every role, account or input works correctly. If you share only static mockups, label them as mockups and ask about the information they communicate.

Ask a peer to explain the screen before showing the answer

Show a relevant reviewer the empty view and ask what they think has happened and what they would do next. For the fictional first-use screen, they might expect incoming requests to appear automatically. That interpretation would reveal a gap if the real product requires manual creation.

For the filtered-empty view, ask what they expect the clear-filter action to change. Avoid telling them the intended meaning before they answer. If they think it deletes requests, investigate the wording and placement rather than treating a polite “looks good” as sufficient review.

I build Buildside. Its public description includes founders sharing progress and finding concrete help. A pair of clearly labelled empty states gives peers a specific review task. Their interpretation remains feedback to investigate; it is not evidence that the whole onboarding experience has been validated.

Check the interaction as well as the explanation

Inspect the action through the input methods your product supports. A visible control should be operable, have a meaningful name and lead to the described route. Geist specifically calls for real buttons or links for empty-state actions. A styled piece of text that cannot be reached or activated would undermine the guidance.

Check the state after the action too. If creating the first request leaves the empty message visible, the walkthrough has uncovered a mismatch between the content and the result. If clearing one filter leaves another active, the message should still reflect the remaining conditions.

You can document these checks without turning the public article into a test report for every interface state. State which route was examined, which methods were used and which related paths remain unchecked. Keep the claim proportional to the work performed.

Publish the condition beside the picture

Give each screenshot or recording a caption that explains the state. For the fictional tracker: “New workspace before its first request” and “Existing workspace with a filter that matches no requests.” These captions make the distinction visible even when an image travels outside its original thread.

If you change the message after review, explain the specific correction. Perhaps the first-use state now says that a person must create a request, or the no-results state now makes the active filter easier to identify. Describe the change without inventing an activation improvement that you have not measured.

For your next public demo, add the screen a new or temporarily blocked reader would actually encounter. Give it a truthful reason for being empty, one useful next action and a checkable result. The populated dashboard can still show the destination; the empty view explains how a person starts or finds their way back.

Hey I'm Uriel Bitton. I write about building in public strategies and growing startups.

Subscribe for more stories on growing your audience by building in public.

Join us on Buildside: the social network for founders building in public.

Sources

Empty states — Vercel Geist Design System
