  • Also by me: Thinking in Go (2-book series) — Complete Guide to Go Programming + Hexagonal Architecture in Go
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

On October 8, 2026, Google Cloud Storage in us-central1 spent twelve and a half hours returning errors and timeouts on writes. Google's incident report puts the impact from 04:00 to 16:30 US/Pacific, which is 11:00 to 23:30 UTC. Every status update posted during the day carried the same line under Workaround: "None at this time."

Then it came back. The final report adds a second window on October 9, 04:05 to 09:46 Pacific, in the us-central1-b zone, for a total of 18 hours and 11 minutes.

If your service writes user uploads or exports straight to a bucket in that region, that was up to 18 hours in which any write could come back as a 503 or hang until your timeout fired, and the writes that did succeed were slow. Google's load balancer is not yours to fix; what your process does with the bytes when the bucket says no is.

The answer fits in plain Node. Failed writes land in a bounded spool on local disk; a drainer pushes them back with jittered retries once the bucket recovers; a gauge shows how deep the backlog is. It all runs against a fake bucket you can break on command, so you can watch the spool fill and empty.

What the report says, and why your client's retries run out

The report is specific. A "traffic sorting optimization configuration update" to the Cloud Storage load-balancing layer bypassed capacity-aware routing and pushed write traffic onto low-capacity backend nodes, which ran out of resources. A separate metadata database issue added errors on top. Engineers tried to add emergency capacity, but per the report "this was blocked by systemic regional capacity limits." The October 9 recurrence came from an incomplete rollback of an upload planner feature.

What clients saw: "Customers primarily observed HTTP 503 UNAVAILABLE errors on WriteObject operations and client-side timeouts." Reads were hit less. Other regions were fine.

The official client's answer to a 503 is on the Cloud Storage retry strategy page, which lists 408, 429 and 5xx responses, plus socket timeouts, as retryable, and recommends exponential backoff with jitter. The Node.js defaults on that page: 3 retries, a 1-second initial wait, a multiplier of 2, a 64-second maximum wait, and a 600-second overall deadline. Uploads are only retried automatically when they are idempotent, meaning you passed an ifGenerationMatch precondition.

So the client gives up after three retries, or ten minutes at the very most. Against a twelve-hour outage, in-request retries are a rounding error. Past that point, the bytes have to live somewhere other than the request, and they have to survive a process restart, because over twelve hours you will deploy, scale, or crash at least once.


When the bucket stops accepting writes, the bytes need a place to wait that outlives the request.

A bounded spool on disk

The spool is a directory. One file per pending object. Each file holds a one-line JSON header with the object name, then the raw bytes. Three rules keep it honest:

  • Write to a temp file, then rename. A crash mid-write leaves a .tmp file that init() deletes, never a half-written entry the drainer would choke on.
  • Cap both file count and bytes. A spool without a cap turns a storage outage into a full-disk outage on your own host.
  • Reserve capacity before the first await. Twenty concurrent failures must not all pass the cap check and then all write. 
// spool.mjs
import {
  mkdir, readdir, readFile, rename, rm, stat, writeFile,
} from 'node:fs/promises';
import { join } from 'node:path';
import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto';

export class SpoolFullError extends Error {}

export class Spool {
  constructor(dir, { maxBytes, maxFiles }) {
    this.dir = dir;
    this.maxBytes = maxBytes;
    this.maxFiles = maxFiles;
    this.bytes = 0;
    this.files = 0;
  }

  async init() {
    await mkdir(this.dir, { recursive: true });
    for (const f of await readdir(this.dir)) {
      const path = join(this.dir, f);
      if (f.endsWith('.tmp')) {
        await rm(path, { force: true });
      } else if (f.endsWith('.spool')) {
        this.bytes += (await stat(path)).size;
        this.files += 1;
      }
    }
  }

  async put(name, data) {
    const head = Buffer.from(JSON.stringify({ name }) + '\n');
    const body = Buffer.concat([head, data]);
    if (this.files + 1 > this.maxFiles ||
        this.bytes + body.length > this.maxBytes) {
      throw new SpoolFullError(`spool full: ${this.files}`);
    }
    // reserve first, so concurrent puts respect the cap
    this.files += 1;
    this.bytes += body.length;
    const id = `${Date.now()}-${randomUUID()}`;
    const final = join(this.dir, `${id}.spool`);
    const tmp = `${final}.tmp`;
    try {
      await writeFile(tmp, body, { flush: true });
      await rename(tmp, final);
    } catch (err) {
      this.files -= 1;
      this.bytes -= body.length;
      await rm(tmp, { force: true });
      throw err;
    }
  }

  async list() {
    const names = await readdir(this.dir);
    return names.filter((f) => f.endsWith('.spool')).sort();
  }

  async oldestAgeMs() {
    const [first] = await this.list();
    return first ? Date.now() - Number(first.split('-')[0]) : 0;
  }

  async oldest() {
    const [first] = await this.list();
    if (!first) return null;
    const path = join(this.dir, first);
    const buf = await readFile(path);
    const nl = buf.indexOf(10); // the header ends at the first \n
    const { name } = JSON.parse(buf.subarray(0, nl).toString());
    const data = buf.subarray(nl + 1);
    return { path, name, data, size: buf.length };
  }

  async remove(entry) {
    await rm(entry.path);
    this.files -= 1;
    this.bytes -= entry.size;
  }
}

flush: true makes writeFile call sync() on the handle before closing it, so the bytes are on disk before the rename publishes the entry. The option landed in Node v21.0.0 and v20.10.0 per the Node fs docs. File names start with Date.now(), so a lexical sort gives you oldest-first, and the age of the oldest entry falls out of the name without opening the file. JSON.stringify escapes newlines inside the object name, so the first raw \n in the file always ends the header.

The upload path is short. Try the bucket with a timeout. If the failure is one a retry could fix, spool it. If the spool is full, put throws SpoolFullError and your caller decides what to do, which is the backpressure: return a 503 to your own client, pause a consumer, stop reading from a queue. The one thing you must not do is drop the write silently.

// uploader.mjs
const WRITE_TIMEOUT_MS = 2_000;
const NET = ['ECONNRESET', 'ETIMEDOUT', 'EPIPE'];

export function isRetryable(err) {
  if (err?.name === 'TimeoutError') return true;
  if (NET.includes(err?.code)) return true;
  const status = Number(err?.code);
  return status === 408 || status === 429 || status >= 500;
}

export async function upload(bucket, spool, name, data) {
  try {
    await bucket.write(name, data, {
      signal: AbortSignal.timeout(WRITE_TIMEOUT_MS),
    });
    return 'stored';
  } catch (err) {
    if (!isRetryable(err)) throw err;
    await spool.put(name, data); // may throw SpoolFullError
    return 'spooled';
  }
}

The retryable set mirrors Google's list: 408, 429, 5xx, and timeouts. A 403 or 404 is a bug in your code or config, and spooling it would hide that bug for hours. AbortSignal.timeout() gives you a signal that aborts after the given milliseconds with a TimeoutError as its reason, which is what isRetryable checks for.

Drain with full jitter

The drainer is one loop. Take the oldest entry, try to write it, delete it on success. On a retryable failure, sleep a random amount between zero and an exponentially growing ceiling. That is the "full jitter" variant from Marc Brooker's Exponential Backoff and Jitter post on the AWS Architecture Blog. When a region comes back, every client that spooled is about to retry at once. Randomized sleeps spread that herd out instead of hitting the recovering backend in synchronized waves.

// drainer.mjs
import { isRetryable } from './uploader.mjs';

const sleep = (ms) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms));

export async function drain(bucket, spool, opts = {}) {
  const {
    baseMs = 250, capMs = 30_000, idleMs = 1_000,
    timeoutMs = 5_000, signal,
  } = opts;
  let failures = 0;
  while (!signal?.aborted) {
    const entry = await spool.oldest();
    if (!entry) {
      await sleep(idleMs);
      continue;
    }
    try {
      await bucket.write(entry.name, entry.data, {
        signal: AbortSignal.timeout(timeoutMs),
      });
      await spool.remove(entry);
      failures = 0;
    } catch (err) {
      if (!isRetryable(err)) throw err;
      failures += 1;
      const ceiling = Math.min(capMs, baseMs * 2 ** failures);
      await sleep(Math.random() * ceiling); // full jitter
    }
  }
}

One drainer per process, writing one entry at a time, is deliberately slow. A recovering storage backend is the worst place to aim a burst. If your backlog is large enough that serial draining takes too long, run a small fixed number of these loops over disjoint entries, not a Promise.all over the whole directory.


Full jitter: each retry waits a random slice of a growing window, so recovering clients don't arrive in lockstep.

The real bucket adapter has one more task beyond calling the client: make the write safe to repeat. A write that timed out on your side may still have landed on Google's side. With ifGenerationMatch: 0, the request preconditions docs say the write only succeeds if no live object with that name exists, and fails with 412 Precondition Failed otherwise. For an object name that is unique per upload, a 412 on a retry means "your earlier attempt worked," so the adapter treats it as success. The preconditionOpts shape is the one Google's Node upload sample uses.

// gcs-bucket.mjs
import { Storage } from '@google-cloud/storage';

function abortable(promise, signal) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    if (signal.aborted) return reject(signal.reason);
    signal.addEventListener(
      'abort', () => reject(signal.reason), { once: true },
    );
    promise.then(resolve, reject);
  });
}

export class GcsBucket {
  constructor(bucketName) {
    this.bucket = new Storage().bucket(bucketName);
  }

  async write(name, data, { signal }) {
    const save = this.bucket.file(name).save(data, {
      resumable: false,
      preconditionOpts: { ifGenerationMatch: 0 },
    });
    try {
      await abortable(save, signal);
    } catch (err) {
      if (err?.code === 412) return; // an earlier try landed
      throw err;
    }
  }
}

abortable stops your code from waiting. It does not cancel the HTTP request underneath, which is why the adapter sends the precondition: the abandoned request can still succeed later, and the next attempt has to cope with that. The status-on-err.code check matches how the client's ApiError carries the HTTP status. Confirm it against the client version you pin, because a wrong check here turns every successful retry into a 412 that stops the drainer, with the entry still on disk.

Watch it fill and drain

The fake bucket fails on command. While failing is true, half its writes throw a 503 and the other half hang until the caller's timeout fires, which matches the two symptoms in Google's report.

// fake-bucket.mjs
export class FakeBucket {
  objects = new Map();
  failing = false;

  async write(name, data, { signal }) {
    if (this.failing) {
      if (Math.random() < 0.5) {
        const err = new Error('503 UNAVAILABLE');
        err.code = 503;
        throw err;
      }
      await new Promise((_, reject) => {
        if (signal.aborted) return reject(signal.reason);
        signal.addEventListener(
          'abort', () => reject(signal.reason), { once: true },
        );
      });
    }
    this.objects.set(name, Buffer.from(data));
  }
}

The metrics endpoint exposes the three numbers you will alert on, in the Prometheus text exposition format. No client library needed.

// metrics.mjs
import { createServer } from 'node:http';

export function serveMetrics(spool, port = 9464) {
  return createServer(async (req, res) => {
    if (req.url !== '/metrics') return res.writeHead(404).end();
    const age = (await spool.oldestAgeMs()) / 1000;
    res.writeHead(200, {
      'content-type': 'text/plain; version=0.0.4',
    });
    res.end([
      '# TYPE upload_spool_files gauge',
      `upload_spool_files ${spool.files}`,
      '# TYPE upload_spool_bytes gauge',
      `upload_spool_bytes ${spool.bytes}`,
      '# TYPE upload_spool_oldest_age_seconds gauge',
      `upload_spool_oldest_age_seconds ${age}`,
      '',
    ].join('\n'));
  }).listen(port);
}

The demo produces 50 writes a second, breaks the bucket from second 2 to second 8, and stops producing at second 10. The spool is capped at 200 files, which a six-second outage at that rate overflows on purpose, so you also see backpressure kick in.

// demo.mjs  (Node 20.10+; run: node demo.mjs)
import { FakeBucket } from './fake-bucket.mjs';
import { Spool, SpoolFullError } from './spool.mjs';
import { upload } from './uploader.mjs';
import { drain } from './drainer.mjs';
import { serveMetrics } from './metrics.mjs';

const bucket = new FakeBucket();
const spool = new Spool('./spool-data', {
  maxBytes: 5 * 1024 * 1024,
  maxFiles: 200,
});
await spool.init();

const stop = new AbortController();
const drainer = drain(bucket, spool, {
  signal: stop.signal, capMs: 2_000,
});
const metrics = serveMetrics(spool);

let n = 0;
const counts = { stored: 0, spooled: 0, rejected: 0 };
const producer = setInterval(async () => {
  const name = `events/${n++}.json`;
  const data = Buffer.from(JSON.stringify({ n, at: Date.now() }));
  try {
    counts[await upload(bucket, spool, name, data)] += 1;
  } catch (err) {
    if (!(err instanceof SpoolFullError)) throw err;
    counts.rejected += 1;
  }
}, 20);

const report = setInterval(() => {
  console.log(
    `depth=${spool.files} in_bucket=${bucket.objects.size}`,
    JSON.stringify(counts),
  );
}, 500);

setTimeout(() => { bucket.failing = true; }, 2_000);
setTimeout(() => { bucket.failing = false; }, 8_000);
setTimeout(() => clearInterval(producer), 10_000);
setTimeout(async () => {
  stop.abort();
  clearInterval(report);
  metrics.close();
  await drainer;
  console.log('final depth', spool.files);
}, 20_000);

What to look for in the log lines: depth sits at 0 for two seconds, climbs once the bucket breaks, hits the 200 cap, and rejected starts counting. After second 8 the drainer's next attempt succeeds, its failure counter resets, and depth falls back to 0. On a clean run, the number to check at the end is that in_bucket equals stored + spooled: everything the spool accepted made it to the bucket, and everything it refused was reported to the caller, not lost. While it runs, curl localhost:9464/metrics shows the gauges move. Kill the process mid-outage and start it again, and init() picks the backlog up from disk.

Alert on the age, not only the depth. A deep spool that is draining is fine. A shallow spool whose oldest entry is two hours old means the drainer is stuck.

- alert: UploadSpoolStuck
  expr: upload_spool_oldest_age_seconds > 900
  for: 5m
- alert: UploadSpoolNearlyFull
  expr: upload_spool_bytes > 0.8 * 5242880
  for: 2m

Where this stops helping

The spool needs a disk that survives the process. On Cloud Run, the container contract says the writable filesystem "is an in-memory file system, so writing to it uses the instance's memory," and that data written to it "doesn't persist when the instance stops." A spool there eats your memory limit and dies with the instance. Same story for a Kubernetes emptyDir when the pod is deleted. You want a persistent volume, or a VM disk.

Ordering is not preserved. While the spool drains, fresh writes go straight to the bucket and overtake older spooled ones. If a consumer depends on write order, route every write through the spool whenever it is non-empty.

list() reads the whole directory on every drain step. That is fine for thousands of entries and wasteful for millions. At that scale, keep an in-memory index built at init() or move to an append-only log with an offset file.

A poison entry blocks the line. If a spooled object keeps failing with a non-retryable error, the drainer throws and stops, and the age alert above is how you find out. Decide up front whether such entries get moved to a dead-letter directory or need a human.

And the spool lives in the same failure domain as your host. If the zone that holds your disk is the one having a bad day, the backlog waits with it. A second bucket in another region is the other half of this design, and it costs you reconciliation logic on read. The spool buys you hours of not losing data. It doesn't replace that decision.

If this was useful

The spool is a small instance of an old idea: when a dependency is down, absorb the load in a bounded buffer, push back on callers when the buffer fills, and recover gently with jittered retries. The System Design Pocket Guide: Fundamentals covers those building blocks, from queues and backpressure to retries, timeouts and availability trade-offs, so you can reach for the right one before the next status page says "None at this time."

articles.title: OpenTelemetry JS 3.0 just shipped. I tested both lines side by side. Here's what broke.
articles.description: TL;DR - On October 20, OpenTelemetry JS shipped @opentelemetry/api 1.10 and SDK 3.0. I was building...
articles.body_html:
TL;DR - On October 20, OpenTelemetry JS shipped @opentelemetry/api 1.10 and SDK 3.0. I was building a library that has to work with whatever OTel setup an app already has, so I ran the same test suite against both lines. I found three breaking changes, a peer range split that one dependency can't span, an app quietly running two copies of the OTel API, and a Node 24 behavior that contradicts the Node 24 docs. Everything below is reproduced in code.

Why I had to care about both lines

I'm building a test library for AI agents. It records OpenTelemetry gen_ai.* spans while a test runs and asserts on what the agent did. The hard requirement: never break the app's own telemetry. No replaced providers, no fighting over globals, and the app should export exactly the same spans with or without my library.

That means I don't get to pick an OTel version. The app picks it. And as of this week, apps are split:

Line API SDK sdk-node
Legacy ≤ 1.9 2.x (2.12) 0.2xx (0.223)
Modern 1.10 3.0 0.300

So I wrote a spike that runs the same 27 scenarios on both lines, with Vercel AI SDK 7 as the instrumentation. Here's what came out.

1. Three breaking changes in SDK 3.0

SimpleSpanProcessor takes an options object 

// SDK 2.x
new SimpleSpanProcessor(exporter);

// SDK 3.0
new SimpleSpanProcessor({ exporter });

TypeScript catches this. Plain JavaScript doesn't. With the old call shape on 3.0, nothing throws at construction. Spans just never arrive, and the only trace of the problem is a diag log entry:

TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'export')

forceFlush() then fails with the same error for forceFlush. If your diag logger is off, your traces silently vanish.

sdk-trace-base became sdk-trace, and the provider was renamed

The 3.0 tracing SDK lives in a new package, @opentelemetry/sdk-trace. The old @opentelemetry/sdk-trace-base tops out at 2.12, which is already a thin shim re-exporting from the new package. In 3.0, BasicTracerProvider is gone. The class is now TracerProvider:

// SDK 2.x
import { BasicTracerProvider } from '@opentelemetry/sdk-trace-base';

// SDK 3.0
import { TracerProvider } from '@opentelemetry/sdk-trace';

sdk-node dropped its re-exports

sdk-node 0.2xx re-exported the whole SDK as namespaces, so a lot of setup code looks like this:

import { NodeSDK, tracing } from '@opentelemetry/sdk-node';
const exporter = new tracing.InMemorySpanExporter();

In 0.300, the package exports exactly two things: NodeSDK and startNodeSDK. tracing is undefined, so the line above throws Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'InMemorySpanExporter').

2. One dependency can't span both lines

These are the peer ranges as published:

Package @opentelemetry/api peer range
sdk-trace-base 2.12 >=1.3.0 <1.10.0
sdk-node 0.223 >=1.3.0 <1.10.0
sdk-trace 3.0 >=1.10.0 <1.11.0
sdk-node 0.300 >=1.10.0 <1.11.0
context-async-hooks 3.0 >=1.0.0 <1.11.0

The ranges don't overlap. If a library depends on any SDK package, it supports exactly one line, and every app on the other line gets peer warnings or a second SDK.

My fix was to depend on no SDK at all. The library ships a small in-memory Tracer written against @opentelemetry/api only, and takes the API as a peer dependency, so it always shares the app's copy. That last part turned out to matter more than I expected.

3. Your app may be running two copies of the OTel API

Vercel's @ai-sdk/otel 1.0.150 lists the API as a regular dependency, pinned to an exact version:

"dependencies": {
  "@opentelemetry/api": "1.9.1"
}

Put that in an app on the modern line and you get two copies:

node_modules/@opentelemetry/api                                   → 1.10.0  (the app)
node_modules/.pnpm/@ai-sdk+otel@…/node_modules/@opentelemetry/api → 1.9.1   (@ai-sdk/otel)

It still works, and the reason is worth knowing. OTel keeps its globals (tracer provider, context manager, propagator) on a shared global object, and every API copy checks the registered version before using it. Within a major version, the rule in api/src/internal/semver.ts boils down to:

// A copy may use a global only if the global was registered by the same or a NEWER minor.
ownVersion.minor <= globalVersion.minor

So an older copy can read globals registered by a newer one, but not the other way around. I checked both directions with two API copies side by side:

Global registered by Read by Result
API 1.10 API 1.9 ✅ sees the registered context manager
API 1.9 API 1.10 ❌ gets a no-op manager, the value is silently lost

The modern line plus @ai-sdk/otel is the safe direction: the app registers with 1.10, and the SDK reads with 1.9. Now flip it. An app on the legacy line registers with 1.9, and any library that brings its own 1.10 copy gets no-ops. It throws no error and logs no warning. Its spans and context just aren't there.

Check what you have:

pnpm why @opentelemetry/api   # or: npm ls @opentelemetry/api

If you maintain a library: make @opentelemetry/api a peer dependency, never a direct one. That's how you guarantee one copy.

4. Node 24: AsyncLocalStorage.disable() doesn't do what the docs say

OTel's context manager for Node is a thin wrapper around AsyncLocalStorage, and its disable() calls AsyncLocalStorage.disable(). I wrote my own small manager to drop the context-async-hooks dependency (its peer range caps the API below 1.11). CI went green on Node 22 and red on Node 24.

Here's a minimal reproduction:

import { AsyncLocalStorage } from 'node:async_hooks';
import { setTimeout as sleep } from 'node:timers/promises';

const als = new AsyncLocalStorage();
const inFlight = als.run('ctx', async () => {
  await sleep(5);
  return als.getStore();
});
await sleep(1);
als.disable();
console.log(await inFlight);
Runtime Output
Node 22.23 undefined
Node 24.22 'ctx'
Node 24.22 with --no-async-context-frame undefined

The Node 24 docs say that after disable(), "all current contexts linked to the instance will be exited." On Node 24, an operation that's already in flight keeps its store anyway. The cause is AsyncContextFrame, which became the default AsyncLocalStorage implementation in Node 24. Turn it off and you get the documented behavior back.

Who cares? Mostly test suites. A common pattern is afterEach(() => context.disable()). On Node 24, async work that's still running from the previous test can keep its context. My manager now keeps its own disabled flag, so active() returns ROOT_CONTEXT after disable() on every runtime, until the next with().

Two smaller gotchas

  • NodeSDK + SimpleSpanProcessor exports asynchronously. It waits for async resource detection before exporting. A test that reads an InMemorySpanExporter right after a span ends sees zero spans. Call processor.forceFlush() first. I lost a while on this one: my "app exports the same spans" check reported a baseline of 0.
  • pnpm 12 won't install anything published less than a day ago. ai@7.0.153 came out the same afternoon I needed it, and I got ERR_PNPM_MINIMUM_RELEASE_AGE_VIOLATION. Don't bypass it; pin the previous release. That's the supply-chain policy working as intended.

Checklist

  • [ ] Run pnpm why @opentelemetry/api and confirm a single copy, or at least that the app's copy is the newest one.
  • [ ] If you write a library, make the OTel API a peer dependency and don't depend on an SDK package unless you must.
  • [ ] Moving to SDK 3.0: switch to new SimpleSpanProcessor({ exporter }), @opentelemetry/sdk-trace and TracerProvider, and stop importing tracing from sdk-node.
  • [ ] Turn on the diag logger in tests (diag.setLogger). Silent export failures only show up there.
  • [ ] On Node 24, don't rely on AsyncLocalStorage.disable() to cut off in-flight async work.
  • [ ] Compare the shape of exported spans (names, parents, attributes), not just their names. Name-only checks let a changed parent slip through. I learned that from my own code review.

What I'm building

All of this came out of the first spike for toadwright 🐸, a Playwright-style test library for AI agents. You assert on the agent's trajectory (tools called, order, arguments, cost), and every test runs N times, because one green run proves nothing. It's early. The spike, the matrix that runs both OTel lines in CI, and the design decision behind it are public: ADR-001 · repo.

The next post will be about the part that actually matters: what happens when you run the same agent test ten times.

Have you hit the two-copies problem in a real app? I'd love to hear how it showed up. 🐸

articles.title: I replaced npm with pnpm in a monorepo with 14 packages. Here's what actually broke.
articles.description: I moved a Turborepo monorepo with 14 packages from npm to pnpm. The migration took a day and a half....
articles.body_html:
I moved a Turborepo monorepo with 14 packages from npm to pnpm. The migration took a day and a half. Three things broke. Two things improved more than I expected. Here is what happened.

The monorepo

The project is a calculator hub built with Astro 5, React, shadcn/ui, and Tailwind CSS 4. The monorepo has 14 packages:

  • 2 apps (the main site and a documentation site)
  • 4 shared UI packages (components, theme, icons, utils)
  • 3 tooling packages (eslint config, tsconfig, tailwind config)
  • 5 feature packages (individual calculator modules)

Total dependencies: 847 unique packages across all workspaces. With npm, the node_modules directory was 2.3 GB. Install time on a clean cache: 4 minutes 12 seconds.

What broke

1. Hoisting differences broke two packages.

npm hoists all dependencies to the root node_modules by default. pnpm uses a symlinked structure where each package gets its own node_modules with symlinks to a shared store. This means packages can only access dependencies they explicitly declare in their package.json.

Two of my feature packages were importing a utility (clsx) that was not in their package.json. It worked under npm because clsx was hoisted to the root and accessible from anywhere. Under pnpm, the import failed with "Cannot find module 'clsx'".

The fix was to add clsx to the dependencies of both packages. This is the correct behavior: packages should declare what they import. But if you have been relying on npm's hoisting, pnpm will surface every undeclared dependency in your monorepo.

2. The Turborepo cache needed a reset.

After switching package managers, the Turborepo build cache was stale. Builds were passing but using cached outputs from the npm era, which meant the cache hits were masking potential failures. I had to clear the cache with turbo clean and run a full rebuild to get accurate results.

This is not a pnpm bug. It is a consequence of changing anything that affects the build inputs. But it is easy to miss if you assume the cache is still valid after the migration.

3. One postinstall script failed.

A package had a postinstall script that referenced ../../node_modules/.bin/something. Under npm, this path existed because of hoisting. Under pnpm, the binary is in the package's own node_modules/.bin, not the root. The script failed.

The fix was to use npx something or pnpm exec something instead of hardcoding the path. This is a best practice anyway, but legacy scripts that worked under npm's hoisting model needed updating.

What improved

1. Disk usage dropped from 2.3 GB to 410 MB.

pnpm's content-addressable store deduplicates packages across all workspaces. A package that appears in 10 workspaces is stored once on disk and symlinked. The 2.3 GB node_modules became 410 MB. On a CI runner with limited disk space, this alone justified the migration.

2. Install time dropped from 4:12 to 1:38.

On a clean cache, pnpm install took 1 minute 38 seconds versus npm's 4 minutes 12 seconds. On a warm cache (with the store already populated), pnpm install took 22 seconds. The speedup comes from the hard-linking strategy: packages that are already in the global store are linked, not downloaded.

In CI, where each run starts with a clean checkout but the pnpm store can be cached, the warm-cache install time is what matters. Caching ~/.local/share/pnpm/store in GitHub Actions reduced install time from 1:38 to 28 seconds.

3. pnpm why is better than npm ls.

Tracing why a dependency is installed is clearer with pnpm. pnpm why clsx shows the full dependency chain from root to the package that depends on it. npm ls clsx gives a tree that is harder to read in a monorepo with 14 packages.

The migration steps

If you are doing the same migration, here is what worked:

# 1. Delete npm artifacts
rm -rf node_modules **/node_modules package-lock.json **/package-lock.json

# 2. Enable pnpm
corepack enable
corepack prepare pnpm@latest --activate

# 3. Install
pnpm install

# 4. Fix undeclared dependencies (pnpm will tell you which imports fail)
# 5. Clear Turborepo cache
npx turbo clean

# 6. Full rebuild
pnpm run build

Step 4 is where most of the time goes. pnpm will fail on every undeclared import. Each failure is a package you need to add to a package.json that should have declared it in the first place.

What I would do differently

Run pnpm install --shamefully-hoist first to get a baseline. The --shamefully-hoist flag mimics npm's hoisting behavior, so the install will succeed without fixing undeclared dependencies. This gives you a working baseline. Then remove the flag and fix the failures one by one, testing after each fix.

Check postinstall scripts before migrating. Any script that references ../../node_modules paths will break. Find them with grep -r "node_modules" --include="*.js" packages/ and fix them before switching.

Cache the pnpm store in CI from day one. The install time difference between cached and uncached is 28 seconds vs 1:38. Over a week of CI runs, that is hours saved.

Is it worth it?

For a monorepo with 14 packages, yes. The disk space and install time improvements are immediate and significant. The migration cost is a day and a half of fixing undeclared dependencies, which is work that should have been done anyway.

For a single-package project, the benefit is smaller. The install time and disk improvements are proportional to the number of packages and the amount of dependency overlap. A single app with no shared dependencies will see a smaller speedup.

The undeclared dependency issue is the main friction. If your monorepo has been relying on npm's hoisting for years, pnpm will surface every place where a package imports something it does not declare. That is painful in the short term and correct in the long term.

articles.title: After Effects, but inside a browser tab (free, no install)
articles.description: AtomCut is a free After Effects alternative in a browser tab: curves, expressions, tracking, depth, rigs, physics and 3D, mapped tool by tool.
articles.body_html:
AtomCut is a free motion design and video studio that runs in a browser tab. If you know After Effects, you already know most of it: compositions, keyframes, a graph editor, expressions, tracking, rigs, 3D. The difference is where it lives. You open a URL and start keyframing. No installer, no account, no Creative Cloud updater asking to restart.

This post maps the After Effects workflow onto AtomCut, tool by tool, with screenshots from the editor as it is today (version 4.17). It also lists where After Effects is still the better choice, because there are real ones.


A tracker on the cabin (97% confidence across the clip), and a label riding it. The green strip under the clip on the timeline is the tracked span.

What does each After Effects tool map to?

In After Effects In AtomCut Notes
Composition, precomp Frame, nested comp Frames sit side by side on an infinite canvas, like artboards in Figma. Nest one inside another and it plays as a clip.
Graph Editor Curves panel Speed and value curves, eased handles, every keyed property in one view.
Hold keyframe Hold easing Drawn as a step in Curves, and kept as a hold in Lottie.
Expressions Expressions in any field Type wiggle(2, 10) or layer("Title").x + 40 into a field and press Enter.
Tracker, Mocha Track tab Point, Object, Surface (corner pin) or Outline.
3D Camera Tracker Camera track Solves the move and the lens, then builds a 3D scene behind your footage.
Rotobrush for "text behind a person" Depth track + Behind No masks to paint. More on this below.
Duik, RubberHose Bones, IK, Character tab Rigging, poses, blinking and lip sync are built in.
Newton (plugin) Physics Gravity, collisions, joints, forces. Built in.
Element 3D, Cinema 4D Lite 3D worlds Meshes, lights, materials, extruded text, sculpting.
Bodymovin Lottie export With a fidelity report of anything that did not translate.
ExtendScript Scripts panel Plain JavaScript: await ac.layer.create({…}).

Most of these sit one click away from the layer you selected, in the tabs on the right: Design, Effects, Animate, Track, Physics, Sound.

Is there a graph editor?

Yes. Select a layer, open Curves under the timeline, and every keyed property is drawn as a curve you can shape. Below, a title fades in, drops 100 px and settles from 82% to 100% scale. Three properties, three easings, one view.


Curves: Scale, Y and Opacity keyed on one title, each with its own ease.

Easings have names you can type (ease-out-expo, ease-in-out-back, cubic-bezier(…)), so a curve you liked is a string you can copy into another project. Record mode keys every edit you make while it is on, the way After Effects' stopwatch does once you have clicked it.

Can I write expressions?

Every field that holds a value can hold a formula instead. Click a field, type wiggle(2, 10) or #layer.rotation * 2, press Enter, and it turns purple. Other layers are read by name: layer("Title").x + 40 keeps one layer 40 px to the right of another.

Two details After Effects users tend to like. Expressions are typed (number, vector, colour, text, layer), so a formula that returns the wrong kind of value shows an error while you type, not at render time. And if a formula breaks, the field keeps its last good value and turns red instead of throwing your layer to 0,0.

A tracker is readable the same way: track("Cabin").position is the cabin's position on the current frame. The same values are available on the node board, if you think in wires.

How does tracking work?

Open the Track tab on a video or picture and draw around what you want to follow: a box, an oval, a polygon or a pen outline. It tracks both directions from that frame while you watch the outline ride the footage. Then pick what to do with it: stick a layer on it, stabilize the shot, blur or grade a moving region, or read it in an expression.

The screenshot at the top is that whole loop. The cabin was drawn once on the first frame; the label follows it through the camera move; the Track tab says 97% confidence and lists the label under Used by. When a track drifts, drag the outline back onto the subject on that one frame. The stretch around your fix re-tracks by itself and lands on it, and the fix survives every later re-track.

Trackers belong to the footage, not the clip. Split it, trim it, speed it up, and the track stays glued to the picture. Drop the same file into another project and it is already tracked.

For shots where the camera itself moves, a Camera track solves where the camera went and what lens it used, and Make 3D scene turns that into a 3D world with your footage behind it. Click three points on the floor to level it, then stand a title on a wall or a table and it stays put as the camera moves. It needs real parallax over rigid scenery: a locked-off pan solves as a tripod shot, and a frame full of moving water will not solve.

How do I put text behind a person or a mountain?

In After Effects this is a rotoscoping job: paint a mask on the subject, refine it, fix the frames where it slips. In AtomCut, add a Depth track to the footage. Every pixel gets a distance from the lens, worked out on your own machine (on the GPU when there is one). Then add Behind to the title, and whatever stands in front of it in the shot covers it.


One effect card, Behind, on the title. The peak in front covers the letters; nothing was masked by hand.

The cover of this post is that frame, exported. The same depth drives three more things: Fog that thickens with distance, Lens blur that focuses at a depth (key the focus to rack it), and grade windows that select a band of depth, so you can cool the background and lift the subject without drawing anything.

The depth model downloads once, the first time you use it (60 to 130 MB depending on your machine), and is kept on the device across app updates. After that it works offline. On an M1 MacBook it took about three minutes for an 8-second 1080p clip.

What about characters, physics and 3D?

These are the places where After Effects users usually buy plugins, and where AtomCut ships the feature in the box.


Physics on a title: it falls, lands on the shelf, and the shapes pile up around it. The Physics tab holds body, bounce, friction and forces.

  • Physics. Give any layer a body in the Physics tab and it drops, lands and settles. A star lands on its points and a word on its letters. Every frame is a function of time, so you can scrub backwards through a collision.
  • Characters. Draw bones through your art, and dragging a hand pulls the arm along (IK). The Character tab holds poses for mouths, eyes, brows and hands. Give a character a voice clip and its mouth follows; fix one syllable by hand and the fix stays.
  • 3D worlds. A world is a comp with depth: meshes, lights, materials, extruded text, sculpting and drawing in 3D. It renders on the same timeline as everything else.


A bone with Follow on: the antenna trails the hop and settles by itself. Five frames from a render.

Where is After Effects still the better tool?

Honestly, in several places:

  • Heavy footage. A browser tab works within the browser's memory. Long 4K timelines with many layers of video are After Effects (or DaVinci) territory. AtomCut is built for motion graphics, social video and UI animation, not for finishing a feature film.
  • The plugin and template ecosystem. Twenty years of Trapcode, Element and marketplace templates do not exist here.
  • The pipeline. If your studio hands .aep files around, AtomCut does not open them.
  • Tutorials. Every After Effects problem has a ten-year-old YouTube video. AtomCut has its docs and a changelog.

The free editor has every tool, but exports video up to 720p. Full HD and 4K, transparent video and the AI agent link are in Pro: $29 a year with a 7-day free trial, or $59 once for the first 300 buyers.

Can an AI agent drive it?

Yes, and this part has no After Effects equivalent yet. AtomCut speaks MCP, so Claude Code or any MCP client can build scenes, track footage, rig characters and render frames in the editor while you watch, each request one undo step. Every screenshot in this post came out of that same scripting surface: the scenes were built by script in a real editor, then captured. That is a Pro feature; the Scripts panel, where you write the JavaScript yourself, is free.

FAQ

Is AtomCut a free After Effects alternative? The editor is free with no account and no watermark, and exports up to 720p. Pro adds HD and 4K export for $29 a year (7-day free trial) or $59 once.

Does it open After Effects projects? No. It exports MP4, WebM, GIF, PNG sequences, SVG, Lottie and PDF.

Does it work offline? Yes. Once the editor has loaded on a device, it keeps working without a connection, and there are desktop apps for macOS, Windows and Linux.

Can it do motion tracking and text behind a subject? Yes: point, object, surface and outline tracking, a camera solve, and depth-based Behind, Fog and Lens blur. See the tracking docs.

Does it have expressions like After Effects? Yes, in any field, including wiggle(). See expressions and the full capability list.

Open AtomCut in a tab: app.atomcut.net

articles.title: What a CORS error actually means, and how I fix each Chrome message
articles.description: TL;DR: A CORS error means the browser refused to give your page a response from another origin,...
articles.body_html:
TL;DR: A CORS error means the browser refused to give your page a response from another origin, because the server didn't send an Access-Control-Allow-Origin header that allows you. The fix lives on the server, or in a dev proxy so the browser only talks to its own origin. The text after has been blocked by CORS policy: in the Console tells you which header to fix. If the request sends JSON or an Authorization header, look at the OPTIONS preflight first. The Network panel files it under Other, so the Fetch/XHR filter hides it.

The 30-second version of CORS

  • An origin is scheme + host + port. localhost:5173 and localhost:8080 are different origins.
  • The browser enforces CORS. Postman and curl don't, which is why "it works in Postman" tells you nothing.
  • The server opts in by sending Access-Control-Allow-Origin and friends. Your frontend can't grant itself access.
  • JSON bodies, Authorization headers and methods other than GET/HEAD/POST trigger a preflight: an OPTIONS request, sent without cookies or tokens, asking whether the real request is allowed.

Read the message, not the TypeError

In code you only get TypeError: Failed to fetch (or Axios's Network Error). The browser hides the reason from scripts on purpose. The Console has the real message:

Access to fetch at 'https://api.example.com/orders' from origin 'http://localhost:5173'
has been blocked by CORS policy: No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is present
on the requested resource.

Here's what I do for each ending Chrome prints. The strings come from Chromium's cors_error_string.cc:

Message ends with Fix
No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is present on the requested resource. Send the header. If the response was a 401/404/500, your error path probably skips the CORS middleware.
It does not have HTTP ok status. (preflight) The OPTIONS request got a non-2xx response. Usually auth middleware rejecting a preflight that has no token. Answer OPTIONS with 204 before auth.
Redirect is not allowed for a preflight request. The preflight hit a 301/302/307. Use the final URL (trailing slash, https, login redirect).
...must not be the wildcard '*' when the request's credentials mode is 'include'. You send cookies. Echo the exact origin, add Vary: Origin.
...'Access-Control-Allow-Credentials' header in the response is '' which must be 'true'... Add Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true.
Request header field authorization is not allowed by Access-Control-Allow-Headers in preflight response. Add the header to Access-Control-Allow-Headers.
Method PUT is not allowed by Access-Control-Allow-Methods in preflight response. Add the method to Access-Control-Allow-Methods.
...has a value '...' that is not equal to the supplied origin. Allow list has the wrong origin. Check port, scheme, www.
...contains multiple values '*, *', but only one is allowed. Both nginx and the app add the header. Remove one.

Finding the preflight in DevTools

  1. Open DevTools before reproducing. Tick Preserve log if a redirect clears the list.
  2. In the Network panel, pick All instead of Fetch/XHR.
  3. The blocked request shows CORS error in the Status column (Chrome 88+). Hover it for the reason code, e.g. PreflightInvalidStatus.
  4. The preflight is its own OPTIONS row with Type preflight. Check its status, then compare Access-Control-Request-Method / -Headers in the request with Access-Control-Allow-* in the response.
  5. No preflight row? The request was simple, or Chrome used a cached result (Access-Control-Max-Age, capped at 7200 s in Chrome). Tick Disable cache and retry.

Then I replay the preflight with curl, which shows exactly what the server returns:

curl -i -X OPTIONS 'https://api.example.com/orders' \
  -H 'Origin: http://localhost:5173' \
  -H 'Access-Control-Request-Method: POST' \
  -H 'Access-Control-Request-Headers: authorization, content-type'

To test a fix before touching the server, Chrome 113+ lets you override response headers locally: Network > Headers > Response Headers, edit the value, reload.

Server fixes

Express, mounted before auth:

import cors from "cors";

app.use(cors({
  origin: ["http://localhost:5173", "https://app.example.com"],
  credentials: true, // only if you send cookies
}));
app.use(authMiddleware);

Next.js App Router route handler:

// app/api/orders/route.ts
const ALLOWED = new Set(["http://localhost:5173", "https://app.example.com"]);

const corsHeaders = (origin: string | null): Record<string, string> => ({
  ...(origin && ALLOWED.has(origin) ? { "Access-Control-Allow-Origin": origin } : {}),
  "Access-Control-Allow-Methods": "GET, POST, OPTIONS",
  "Access-Control-Allow-Headers": "Content-Type, Authorization",
  Vary: "Origin",
});

export const OPTIONS = (req: Request) =>
  new Response(null, { status: 204, headers: corsHeaders(req.headers.get("origin")) });

export const GET = async (req: Request) =>
  Response.json({ orders: [] }, { headers: corsHeaders(req.headers.get("origin")) });

For lots of routes, do it once in proxy.ts (middleware.ts before Next 16).

nginx. The always matters, because without it your 401s and 500s go out without the header and surface as CORS errors:

location /api/ {
    if ($request_method = OPTIONS) {
        add_header Access-Control-Allow-Origin "https://app.example.com" always;
        add_header Access-Control-Allow-Methods "GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS" always;
        add_header Access-Control-Allow-Headers "Authorization, Content-Type" always;
        return 204;
    }
    add_header Access-Control-Allow-Origin "https://app.example.com" always;
    add_header Vary Origin always;
    proxy_pass http://backend;
}

On localhost, skip CORS with a proxy

Vite:

// vite.config.ts
export default defineConfig({
  server: {
    proxy: { "/api": { target: "http://localhost:8080", changeOrigin: true } },
  },
});

Next.js:

// next.config.js
module.exports = {
  async rewrites() {
    return [{ source: "/api/:path*", destination: "https://api.example.com/:path*" }];
  },
};

Call fetch("/api/orders") and the browser never makes a cross-origin request. Remember the Vite proxy is dev-only.

Things that look like fixes but aren't

  • mode: "no-cors" gives you an opaque response: status 0, no headers, empty body. It also silently drops Authorization and Content-Type: application/json.
  • --disable-web-security or a "CORS unblock" extension fixes your browser only. Your users still get the error, and your profile is now readable by any site.
  • strict-origin-when-cross-origin is Chrome's default Referrer-Policy (since Chrome 85). It shows up in every request's Headers tab and has nothing to do with CORS.

A faster way to find the preflights

I work on Netraptor, a Chrome extension with its own DevTools panel. In live capture it lists the same requests DevTools records, preflights included, so I filter method:OPTIONS to see every preflight on the page, or is:error for failed calls and 4xx/5xx together. Right-click > Copy > Copy as cURL (bash) gives me the call to replay in a terminal, where CORS doesn't apply.

The full guide, with steps and FAQ: What is a CORS error, and how do you fix it?

articles.title: Knotwork by Rule
articles.description: Knotwork is a page of Insular interlace grown on a grid: one parity rule for over and under, breaks that turn a plait into a knot, pointed corners, a cross-carpet page, and beasts whose heads I couldn't draw, so I traced one.
articles.body_html:
All the plans turn into old tickets, half unredeemed.

Old Tickets

The series has been working its way north. Andalusian tile, then English heraldry, then a medieval English floor, and now the furthest north it's going to get: the carpet pages of the Lindisfarne Gospels, the Book of Durrow and the Book of Kells. Whole pages of vellum given over to ribbons that go over, under, over, under, round every corner and back, in red lead, orpiment yellow and verdigris green, with the odd dog's head biting its own tail.

Knotwork grows those pages from a seed. It's the most rule-bound piece I've made so far, and it turned out the monks had done most of the thinking already.

{{< figure src="https://stepinto.dev/images/knotwork/carpet.webp" class="chart" alt="A wall of manuscript pages, each a plus-shaped cross of green and blue interlace on red, set in a channel, with a second knot of red, yellow and green ribbons filling the bare vellum around it, and small hound heads at the edges" caption="The lindisfarne preset. Seed 698, the year Eadfrith became bishop and, so the story goes, started painting." >}}

Over, under, over, under

If you look closely at the back of a Lindisfarne page you can still find the prick marks and the ruled grid. Interlace was laid out on squares, and once you see that, the rule is short.

Take a grid of squares. Every edge has a midpoint. A strand runs diagonally from one midpoint to the next, so at every midpoint two strands cross. Do nothing else and you get a plain plait. Then pick some edges and make them breaks: a strand that reaches a break turns back off it instead of crossing. The rim of the panel is all breaks, so every strand closes up on itself. Breaks are what turn a plait into a knot, and I chose them by the panel's mirrors so the page stays symmetric, often in runs of two or three along a line, which is where the knot's sharp turns come from.

{{< figure src="https://stepinto.dev/images/knotwork/weave.webp" class="chart" alt="Two rectangles of interlace on cream. On the left an even orange plait with every strand crossing; on the right the same grid in blue with some edges turned into breaks, so the strands loop back into knots" caption="The same six by seven grid. On the left, no breaks, one plait. On the right, three in ten interior edges are breaks." >}}

The bit I was pleased about is over and under. In Çini the strapwork walks each strand from end to end and flips over and under at every crossing it meets. Here there's no walking at all. A crossing on a horizontal edge takes the rising strand over and a crossing on a vertical edge takes the falling one. Every step along a strand lands on the other kind of edge, and every bounce off a break flips its direction, so the alternation round every strand is guaranteed by the grid. In code it's one line:

const over = ((x & 1) === 1) === (dx * dy > 0);

x is in doubled coordinates, where an odd x means a horizontal edge. That's the whole of the weave.

Points in the corners

My first corners were round, and they looked wrong in a way I couldn't name until I went back to the facsimiles. Where a strand turns in a corner of the panel, the scribes draw it up to a sharp point aimed into the corner and back out again. So the page does that now. There's also a "pointed" setting that sharpens every bounce off the rim, which I use for the Kells preset.

{{< figure src="https://stepinto.dev/images/knotwork/bends.webp" class="chart" alt="Three copies of the same blue and green knot. The first has rounded turns everywhere, the second has sharp points in its four corners, the third has points on every turn along the rim as well" caption="Round, corners, pointed. Same knot, three ways to turn at the edge." >}}

The cross-carpet page in the first picture comes from letting a knot fill any region of squares, not just a rectangle. The cross is a plus of knotwork painted on a coloured ground inside a ruled channel, and a second knot fills the bare vellum around it. Then come the frame, its two rules and the red-lead dots. Lindisfarne has a page with over ten thousand of those dots on it, which is the sort of thing that makes you put the pen down for a minute.

The beasts

Insular strands don't always close. Sometimes a ribbon ends in a head, and the head bites something, usually another ribbon or its own tail. On the grid that's a third kind of edge, a cut, where the strand stops instead of turning. Two strand ends always arrive at a cut from the same side, so they pair up neatly: one gets a head, the other becomes the tail it bites.

The head was the problem. I drew mine from curves the way I'd drawn the first lions for Leonor, and it came out like this.

{{< figure src="https://stepinto.dev/images/knotwork/head-drawn.webp" class="chart" alt="A green ribbon ending in a crude head with an eye, two spikes on top like horns and a flap sticking out at the back like a tongue" caption="My drawn head. The question it got was \"what is this meant to be?\", which was fair." >}}

So I did what fixed the lions. I asked an image model for a flat drawing of an Insular hound's head, one gold fill with an even black outline, a red eye, and a piece of blue ribbon gripped in its jaws so I'd know where the bitten strand goes. The neck was to come in from the left as a straight band, cut square, so I could bolt it onto a strand.

{{< figure src="https://stepinto.dev/images/knotwork/head-generated.webp" class="chart" alt="A flat gold hound's head in profile with a red almond eye, a curled lappet off the back of the skull and a long snout, holding a blue ribbon in its open jaws" caption="The drawing I traced. The blue ribbon hanging below the jaw was cut away first, and the bit inside the mouth kept." >}}

The tracer is the forty lines of Node from the heraldry post. I erased the ribbon below the jaw before tracing and kept the piece inside the mouth, which now gets painted in the tail's colour. The rest was placement. My first go pointed the head straight on along its strand, and every beast stuck out of the knot like a dog through a fence. The version that works lets the neck turn off the strand and narrow, so the head lies along the cut facing its tail, and the tail hooks round under the jaw and up into the mouth.

{{< figure src="https://stepinto.dev/images/knotwork/beasts.webp" class="chart" alt="A close view of a knot in split ribbons of red, purple, green and blue on vellum, with four hound heads around it, each lying along the edge with the end of another ribbon curled up into its jaws" caption="The kells preset, close up. Four hounds, each with a tail in its mouth." >}}

Two heads on neighbouring cuts sat on top of each other and looked like a scrum, so no cut is allowed beside another now. A mirror copy that would collide just stays a plain break. The heads are still big for the grid and lie over a strand or two, and at very high zoom there's a faint seam where the neck meets the traced head. I can live with both.

Before the painter

My favourite preset has no colour at all. It's the page as the scribe would have left it for the painter: ink on vellum, ruled frame, a few hounds along the rims.

{{< figure src="https://stepinto.dev/images/knotwork/ink.webp" class="chart" alt="Panels of interlace drawn in brown ink on uncoloured vellum, each in a ruled double frame, with small hound heads along the edges of some panels" caption="The drawing preset. Ink only." >}}

{{< figure src="https://stepinto.dev/images/knotwork/lichfield.webp" class="chart" alt="A large square page of faded red, yellow, green and purple interlace on vellum, with a bare field in the middle where a few hound heads face each other" caption="The lichfield preset, seed 730, the colour gone soft the way that book's has." >}}

In the package

The knots now live in azulejeria as their own module, next to the tile engine but not using any of it. It draws on any 2D canvas.

npm install azulejeria

import { buildKnot, paintKnot } from 'azulejeria/knots';

The README covers the options: masks for crosses and fields, symmetry, cuts, bends, and the traced head with its narrow neck. The knot's grid is the same one under the Mudéjar lacería, so I'd like to see somebody use it for that. Next on the list is Sutton Hoo, which is garnets set in gold cells, and Alicatado's cutter will do most of that work.

articles.title: Stop counting down: the right way to warn users before their session expires
articles.description: The other day I was answering a question about a countdown timer that kept drifting wrong whenever...
articles.body_html:
The other day I was answering a question about a countdown timer that kept drifting wrong whenever the browser tab went into the background. My advice was... okayish. Good enough to be useful, not good enough that I'd want it framed on a wall. So I went back and actually thought it through, and the better answer turned out to be simpler and more correct than what I'd reached for first. Figured it was worth writing up.

The bug everyone hits first

Here's the setup. You've got a session that expires in 30 minutes, and you want to warn the user when they're about 2 minutes away — the classic "Your session is about to expire, stay signed in?" modal.

The obvious way to build this is a countdown:

let remaining = 30 * 60; // seconds

setInterval(() => {
  remaining--;
  render(remaining);
  if (remaining === 120) warnTwoMinutes();
}, 1000);

Run that, switch to another tab for a while, come back, and your timer is wrong. Not late — wrong. It thinks there's more time left than there actually is.

The reason is that browsers throttle setInterval and setTimeout in background tabs to save resources. Chrome got especially aggressive about it starting in Chrome 88, where chained timers in a hidden tab get heavily throttled — we're talking ticks stretched out to once a minute or worse. So while you were away, your remaining-- ran a handful of times instead of hundreds, and the counter never caught up.

The trap is the remaining--. Decrementing assumes every tick happens. The moment ticks get skipped, your value is permanently off by however many you missed.

My first instinct was over-engineered

When I first ran into this, my brain jumped to: move the timer to the server, open a WebSocket, push the state down to the client. The browser can't be trusted to keep time in a background tab, so take the timing out of the browser entirely.

And look — that works. But it's a sledgehammer. You're standing up a persistent connection and a server-side scheduler to solve what is, at heart, an arithmetic mistake. For a countdown to a deadline you already know, that's a lot of moving parts to babysit.

The actual fix: don't count down, compute

The insight that makes the whole problem evaporate: store an absolute deadline, and compute the remaining time on every tick instead of decrementing.

const deadline = Date.now() + 30 * 60 * 1000;

function check() {
  const remaining = deadline - Date.now();
  render(remaining);
  if (remaining <= 120_000) warnTwoMinutes();
}

Now throttling can't corrupt anything. A skipped tick only means check() ran later than you wanted — but whenever it does run, it recomputes from the wall clock and gets the right answer. Late, never wrong. The display in a hidden tab might lag, but it's never lying.

Pair it with one event listener and the background-tab case is genuinely handled:

document.addEventListener("visibilitychange", () => {
  if (document.visibilityState === "visible") check();
});

The instant the user comes back, you recompute and the UI snaps to correct — no matter how badly the timer was throttled while they were gone.

For the 2-minute warning specifically, you can schedule it directly instead of waiting for a tick to cross the line:

setTimeout(warnTwoMinutes, deadline - 120_000 - Date.now());

In the foreground it fires roughly on time; if it's throttled in the background, the visibilitychange recompute catches it when they return. Belt and suspenders.

Where session expiry gets its own personality

Everything above is true for any countdown. But "session expiry" specifically pulls in a few extra concerns, and this is where it got interesting for me.

The deadline isn't yours to make up. The session has a real expiry living server-side. The client's job is to learn it, not invent it — from a JWT's exp claim, a /session endpoint, or a header riding along on requests you're already making. You read it; you don't compute it.

Clock skew suddenly matters a lot. The whole point is to warn before the server kills the session. If the user's laptop clock is three minutes fast, a naive Date.now() countdown warns them after they've already been booted. So anchor to the server's clock once and work off the offset:

function syncSession(serverNow, expiresAt) {
  const skew = serverNow - Date.now();   // how far the client clock is off
  const deadline = expiresAt - skew;     // expiry expressed in client time
  scheduleWarning(deadline);
}

Now the warning fires relative to what the server believes, not what the user's machine believes.

The deadline can move — on purpose. The warning usually comes with a "Stay signed in?" button, and that button extends the session:

warn at (deadline - 2min)
  → show "Stay signed in?" modal
  → button hits the refresh endpoint
  → server returns a NEW expiresAt
  → re-run syncSession() with the new deadline

So your scheduler needs a clear-and-reschedule step, so the old setTimeout gets cancelled when a refresh lands. The deadline isn't drifting — the user is pushing it forward — but your code has to handle it moving either way.

Multiple tabs will embarrass you if you forget them. User has three tabs open, clicks "stay signed in" in one, and two minutes later the other two pop the expiry warning over a session that's perfectly fine. BroadcastChannel is the clean fix:

const channel = new BroadcastChannel("session");

// after a successful refresh:
channel.postMessage({ type: "refreshed", expiresAt: newExpiry, serverNow });

// every tab listens:
channel.onmessage = (e) => {
  if (e.data.type === "refreshed") syncSession(e.data.serverNow, e.data.expiresAt);
};

One tab extends, every tab reschedules. (The older fallback is a storage event on localStorage, but BroadcastChannel is purpose-built and nicer if you don't need to support ancient browsers.)

On return, re-verify instead of trusting your own math. This is the case the original throttling bug actually hides in — a tab backgrounded for a long stretch. The visibilitychange handler should do a little more than recompute, because while the tab was hidden the session might have been refreshed elsewhere, or genuinely expired:

document.addEventListener("visibilitychange", () => {
  if (document.visibilityState === "visible") {
    if (Date.now() >= deadline) handleExpired();   // already gone — just handle it
    else revalidateWithServer();                    // cheap ping; trust the server's answer
  }
});

That's the honest version. The client-side timer is a UX optimization. When the user actually comes back to the tab, asking the server "am I still good?" is more truthful than trusting any local arithmetic.

So when do you need WebSockets?

Not for this. A WebSocket earns its complexity in exactly one scenario here: when the server needs to reach the client unprompted. An admin revokes a session from a dashboard, or it gets killed for a security reason, and you want every open tab to react now rather than at the next page load or visibility check. That's a genuine server-push problem, and a WebSocket (or SSE) is the right tool for it.

But "I know when this expires, warn me before it does" is not a server-push problem. It's an absolute timestamp, a skew correction, and a visibility listener. Same goes for the cookie idea I batted around early on — a cookie's browser-managed auto-expiry deletes the thing at the deadline, which is precisely too late to warn anyone, and there's no "about to expire" event to hook. Cookies are storage, not a scheduler.

The takeaway I keep relearning

The shape of the good solution:

  • Server is the source of truth for when the session ends.
  • Client learns the deadline and corrects for clock skew.
  • Compute remaining time from an absolute deadline — never decrement.
  • Schedule the warning with a stay-signed-in action that can move the deadline.
  • Broadcast refreshes across tabs.
  • Re-verify with the server when the tab becomes visible again.

What I like about this is that the fix wasn't a heavier hammer — it was noticing I'd modeled the problem wrong. I was treating time as something to accumulate tick by tick, when it was sitting right there as a fixed point I could just read against. Most of the timer bugs I've written come down to that same mistake.

There's more to chase here — the refresh-token dance, how this interacts with silent re-auth, what to do when the revalidation ping itself fails — but that's a rabbit hole for another day. I'll leave it on the high note.

articles.title: Running Whisper in the browser: what broke and how I fixed it
articles.description: I run a small site of free browser tools, and the one people use most is a transcriber: you drop in...
articles.body_html:
I run a small site of free browser tools, and the one people use most is a transcriber: you drop in an audio or video file and get text or SRT/VTT subtitles back. By default nothing is uploaded. OpenAI's Whisper runs on your own device through transformers.js, and ffmpeg.wasm pulls the audio out of the file first. (There's also an optional Instant mode that uses the browser's Web Speech API, which sends the audio to Google or Microsoft. It's off by default, and this post is about the on-device mode.)

It worked on my laptop on day one. Making it work on other people's devices took a lot longer. These are the problems that showed up in real use, in the order they hurt, and what I changed.

The setup

  • Audio: ffmpeg.wasm (about 31 MB, downloaded once) converts any file to 16 kHz mono float32 PCM.
  • Speech: transformers.js 4.3 runs Whisper in a Web Worker. I offer three sizes: tiny ("Fast"), base ("Accurate") and small ("Best").
  • Backend: WebGPU when it helps, WASM otherwise. The site doesn't send COOP/COEP headers, so WASM runs single-threaded.

Download sizes, measured from the actual .onnx files on the CDN:

Model WASM (q8) WebGPU (fp16)
tiny 39 MB 73 MB
base 73 MB 139 MB
small 238 MB 463 MB

1. Big videos ran out of memory before transcription even started

The first version did what most ffmpeg.wasm examples do: read the whole file into JavaScript, then write it into ffmpeg's in-memory filesystem. That's two full copies. A 300 MB phone video went past 1 GB of memory just to extract its audio, and phones gave up.

Fix: mount the file with WORKERFS instead of copying it. ffmpeg then reads straight from the File object, chunk by chunk, so the video's size barely matters. Only the extracted audio lives in memory, about 230 MB per hour of float32 PCM. I've since tested a 2.1 GB file. If the mount fails on an old browser, the code falls back to the copy.

2. Always using WebGPU was the wrong default, twice

On phones. Android Chrome exposes navigator.gpu, and the adapter looks fine. But the worker kept dying in the middle of a transcription, probably because of shared memory or unstable drivers: one user in India hit seven failures in a row on the smallest model. Phones now always use WASM with the q8 weights.

On laptops. I assumed the GPU path was faster everywhere. Then I measured on an ordinary 2021 laptop (Core i5-11300H, Intel Iris Xe graphics) with 60 seconds of speech, timing only the transcription step. This was headless Chrome with the Vulkan backend, one run per model, in minutes per 10 minutes of audio:

Model WASM (CPU) WebGPU (Iris Xe)
tiny 2.0 3.4
base 4.0 6.5
small 24.6 86.9

A second run, in headless Chrome with default settings, told the same story for the two smaller models: tiny 2.4 on the CPU against 3.4 on the GPU, base 4.7 against 8.2. I didn't repeat the small model. On that integrated GPU, the processor won every time, by 3.5x on the small model in the first run. Older Intel integrated graphics now go to WASM. The rule checks adapter.info.vendor for intel and an architecture starting with gen-. Newer Intel chips, which I haven't measured, and dedicated GPUs stay on WebGPU.

One detail matters here. transformers.js asks for the high-performance adapter, so the check has to ask for the same one: requestAdapter({ powerPreference: 'high-performance' }). On a laptop with two GPUs, a plain requestAdapter() can return the integrated one while inference runs on the other.

3. The dtype trap

Without an explicit dtype, the WebGPU path downloaded fp32 weights: 923 MB for the small model, without telling anyone. Picking dtypes by hand turned up three things:

  • q8 on the GPU is slow, probably because int8 isn't accelerated there. In an earlier test on the same laptop, with the same model in both runs, a 35-second clip took about 25 s with fp16 and 196 s with q8.
  • fp16 on the GPU is twice the download of q8 but much faster, so it's the GPU default.
  • q4f16 is smaller than q8 for the small model, but it returned unreadable text in my tests. It's out.

On WASM I use q8. Of the formats I tested, it's the smallest that gave readable text. The model repositories also have int8 files that are smaller still, which I haven't tried yet.

4. Failures that should never reach the user

Some errors repeat often enough that showing them is the wrong answer.

  • Out of memory on the larger models. failed to call OrtRun() with an allocation error means the device can't hold that model. The tool now continues by itself with the smallest model and says so on screen, instead of showing a raw ONNX error.
  • Model downloads that stall on slow connections. The tool retries once, and files that finished downloading stay in the browser cache. If it stalls again, it steps down to the next smaller model.
  • A GPU that dies mid-job. The job restarts on the CPU in a fresh worker, and the GPU isn't used again for the rest of that session.

5. Timeouts that fired while work was still happening

In one week, analytics showed four people getting "Reading the audio timed out". The timeout was a fixed 10 minutes, and it started before the 31 MB engine had even downloaded. My best guess is that on a slow connection, the download ate the budget, and files that were still being read failed anyway.

Now the timeout measures lack of progress, not total time. Downloading the engine gets 15 minutes, since it reports no progress. Reading audio only gives up after 3 minutes with no progress event at all.

Phones added one more trap. When you switch apps, the browser freezes the tab, and the timer can fire the moment you come back, before the page has noticed it was hidden. So if the timer fires more than 5 seconds late, or while the page is hidden, it re-arms instead of failing.

6. People leaving halfway

Almost as many people left halfway as hit an error. In one week, 26 people started a transcription: 9 hit an error, and 7 left without any error, before it finished. Several cancelled during the transcription step itself. Small things help:

  • Screen Wake Lock while processing, so a phone screen doesn't turn off and freeze the tab. It's requested again when the page becomes visible, because the browser releases it when the page is hidden.
  • Progress in the tab title, like "42% · Transcribing…", and "✓ Transcript ready" if it finishes while you're on another tab.
  • A beforeunload prompt while a job is running, so an accidental reload doesn't throw away twenty minutes of work.
  • Honest estimates up front. My page used to promise 5–15 minutes per 10 minutes of audio for the small model. The measurement above says 25. The page now shows the measured numbers.

What's still hard

  • The small model on phones is slow. Some languages, like Hindi, Tamil and Urdu, need it to come out right.
  • No speaker labels. Plain Whisper doesn't do diarization.
  • The first run means a download of tens to hundreds of MB, depending on the model. After that, it starts from the cache.

If you want to try it, the tool is at pixthru.com/video-to-text. It has a 12-second sample if you don't want to use your own file. I'd like to hear from anyone who has measured WebGPU against WASM on other GPUs, especially Apple Silicon and AMD integrated graphics.

articles.body_html:
With today's news, I thought I'd share this great program:“When I was growing up in the hills of East Tennessee, I knew my dreams would come true. I know there are children in your community with their own dreams. They dream of becoming a doctor or an inventor or a minister. Who knows, maybe there is a little girl whose dream is to be a writer and singer.The seeds of these dreams are often found in books and the seeds you help plant in your community can grow across the world.”

This is a top-trending Hacker News story with 21 upvotes and 2 comments.
